visual_source_files.evidence: The official README embeds this asset; repository metadata and README title exactly match the paper, and the asset composition matches PDF Figure 1's pipeline and two example strips. It is a rendered asset, not a diagram source.
The official repository tree lists this asset and its dimensions/composition match PDF Figure 3's four-row compression-rate montage. It supplies pixels only, not plotting parameters.
The official README embeds this asset; its rows, columns, values and highlighting match PDF Table 1. It is a rendered table image rather than a generator or LaTeX source.
The official README embeds this dog/mask/usage GIF and its frames match the visual sequence in PDF Figure 5. It is a companion rendered asset, not an exact static source or parameter file.

source_acquisition.search_note: The PDF's project URL is https://research.nvidia.com/labs/dir/infotok/ and the paper states that code is supplementary. gh read-only metadata and README verification selected YWolfeee/InfoTok because its description and README title exactly match the paper. gh recursive-tree and code searches found no paper .tex/.tikz/.pgf, Figure 4 plotting script or table generator; the only savefig/matplotlib hit was a generic tensor-debug utility. Strict-title candidate repositories ZLKong/Awesome-Collection-Token-Reduction and lavinal712/Awesome-Visual-Tokenizers are collections, not the paper's visual source. The four listed assets are therefore rendered_asset evidence for Figures 1, 3, Table 1 and 5 only; all other PDF objects remain without a verified visual source.

paper_style.palette_strategy: Module diagrams use role-specific blue/green/purple/gray fills; Figure 4 fixes red/green/blue method colors; appendix masks use black/white and usage bars use green. Natural video RGB is contextual rather than a shared quantitative encoding.
paper_style.vector_raster_mix: PDF text, captions, table rules and table values are PDF text/line objects, while all six Figures and most in-figure labels are embedded RGB raster images; no verified editable plot or diagram source was found.
paper_style.style_consistency: Caption and table typography is consistent at the PDF-object level, but raster figure labels vary in estimated size and sans-serif treatment. Table 5/6 body text is especially small; method color semantics are not carried consistently from Figure 4 into the montage figures.

figures.label: Figure 1

caption.text: Figure 1: Overall framework of InfoTok, an information-theoretic adaptive video tokenizer. An encoder maps video x into fixed-length embeddings, from which a router estimates the number of tokens N_x based on information complexity (section 3.1). An adaptive compressor encodes the embeddings to N_x tokens (section 3.2). For reconstruction, the tokens are decompressed to fixed-length embeddings and decoded back into video. InfoTok tokenizes based on video complexity: e.g., the stable dog video is compressed more (0.40) than the dynamic cat-fighting video (0.62). Illustration details can be found in Appendix A.

color.semantic_mapping: Green distinguishes encoder/decoder and downstream applications; purple marks the router; blue marks the adaptive compressor/de-compressor; gray marks quantize/de-quantize; pale green marks embeddings; dark blue is the outline and arrow ink.

encodings.x: Left-to-right module sequence from input video through encoder, router, adaptive compressor, quantizer and decompressor to decoder.
encodings.y: Upper pipeline versus lower qualitative video examples and downstream application row; no quantitative y axis.
encodings.color: Module role and direction are redundantly encoded by filled component colors, outlines and labels.
encodings.shape: Rounded rectangles, trapezoid-like compressor blocks and cube-like embedding/token glyphs encode component type.
encodings.line: Solid arrows encode forward and reconstruction data flow.
encodings.facet: Two qualitative example rows separate stable dog and dynamic cat-fighting videos.
encodings.text: Component labels, N_x, x, error and BPP16 annotations identify stages and example values.

figures.data_and_statistics: Conceptual architecture plus two representative video strips. The visible examples report Error 0.0267 and BPP16 compression rate 0.4004 for the stable dog, and Error 0.0438 and rate 0.6168 for cat-fighting; these are point examples, not an aggregate or uncertainty estimate.
figures.evidence_relation: Introduces the router and adaptive compressor interface in section 3.1–3.2, motivates complexity-dependent token length, and points to Appendix A Figures 5–6 for temporal masks; it is a mechanism/interface figure rather than a benchmark result.
design_strengths: The forward and inverse paths make the new router/compressor placement legible in one scan.
Component color, shape and direct labels provide redundant cues and the lower strips connect the abstraction to concrete complexity examples.
The figure supplies a visual bridge from the method claim to later quantitative rate/quality comparisons.
design_weaknesses: Example error and BPP16 values do not define their aggregation, denominator or sampling rule.
Raster labels and module geometry do not have a reusable editable diagram source in the verified repository.
The wide pipeline and small lower thumbnails compete for space at normal PDF zoom.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a single forward/inverse pipeline with an explicit resource-routing block, then place two matched low/high-complexity example strips underneath so the mechanism and its intended visual consequence share one object.

figures.label: Figure 2

caption.text: Figure 2: Reconstructions examples of video with different complexities using different tokenizers. InfoTok-Flex can achieve similar PSNR with much higher compression (compared to Cosmos-DV), and similar compression rates with better PSNR (compared to ElasticTok).

color.semantic_mapping: Natural RGB video carries appearance; dark blue dashed separators divide scenes; black/white labels and red metric emphasis identify rows and selected compression text.

encodings.x: Three scene groups, each containing three ordered video frames.
encodings.y: Method rows: Original, Cosmos-DV, ElasticTok and InfoTok-Flex.
encodings.color: Natural image color shows reconstruction appearance; red selectively emphasizes some compression-rate text.
encodings.shape: Image tiles and row-label bands encode method identity rather than numeric marks.
encodings.line: Vertical dashed separators encode scene boundaries.
encodings.facet: Scene content is the column-group facet; tokenizer is the row facet.
encodings.text: Direct row labels and visible PSNR/BPP16 annotations identify methods and selected values.

figures.data_and_statistics: A 4-by-9 representative reconstruction montage over three scene groups. Visible PSNR/BPP16 text is supplied for Original, Cosmos-DV and ElasticTok (for example 28.97/1.00, 27.09/0.93 and 27.89/0.52 in the first group), while the InfoTok-Flex row has no matching per-row metric labels; no uncertainty or sample-level aggregation is shown.
figures.evidence_relation: Provides qualitative evidence for the same compression-versus-quality comparison summarized in Table 1 and contextualizes the different-complexity claim; it cannot substitute for the aggregate TokenBench/DAVIS evaluation.
design_strengths: Fixed method rows and scene column groups let readers compare spatial reconstruction quality without changing the reading direction.
Three different scene contents make the adaptive-complexity intuition concrete rather than relying on one clip.
Direct labels avoid an external legend for the montage rows.
design_weaknesses: InfoTok-Flex lacks the same-format PSNR/BPP16 labels, so the comparison is not symmetric within the grid.
Only representative scenes are shown and no frame-selection or qualitative assessment protocol is reported.
Natural image color and red text emphasis have no cross-object method-color mapping.
figures.reusable_pattern: Keep Original as the first row, use fixed scene groups as columns and give every method row identical metric annotations so qualitative evidence and budget comparisons can be read without cross-referencing.

figures.label: Figure 3

caption.text: Figure 3: Reconstructions examples of video by InfoTok-Flex with different compression rates.

color.semantic_mapping: Natural RGB reconstruction images carry appearance; dark blue dashed separators divide scenes; black/white direct labels and metric text carry the row and annotation semantics.

encodings.x: Three fixed scene groups with three ordered frames per group.
encodings.y: Original, Rate=0.81, Rate=0.56 and Rate=0.31 rows encode descending compression budgets.
encodings.color: Natural video RGB shows visual degradation; dark blue separators and black/white text are structural cues.
encodings.shape: Uniform image tiles encode frames; no point shape or glyph encoding.
encodings.line: Vertical dashed separators encode scene boundaries.
encodings.facet: Scene group is the facet; compression rate is the row condition.
encodings.text: Direct rate labels and PSNR/BPP16 annotations identify conditions and visible values.

figures.data_and_statistics: One representative video is shown at three scene groups and four rows. Visible PSNR/rate pairs include Original 28.24/.75, 34.87/.63, 33.15/.57; Rate=.81 27.89/.52, 32.98/.44, 33.08/.40; Rate=.56 25.86/.35, 30.33/.25, 26.53/.23. The Rate=.31 row has no corresponding metric annotations; no repetition or uncertainty is shown.
figures.evidence_relation: Isolates the compression-rate mechanism as a qualitative ablation and connects to Figure 4's rate-quality curves and section 4.3; the low-rate row illustrates a possible failure boundary rather than a population estimate.
design_strengths: Holding scenes and tokenizer fixed makes the visual effect of budget reduction easy to attribute.
Rows are ordered from Original/high rate to low rate, exposing where detail begins to disappear.
The verified public compare_length asset corroborates the exact grid composition.
design_weaknesses: The lowest-rate row omits the same metric labels used by the other rows.
One video and three scene groups cannot represent content heterogeneity or a general degradation threshold.
The short caption does not define Rate, BPP16 or the selection of the displayed clip.
figures.reusable_pattern: For a budget ablation, hold frames and scene groups fixed, order rows monotonically by resource rate and keep the quality annotation format identical for every row, including the failure endpoint.

figures.label: Figure 4

caption.text: Figure 4: Video tokenization performance of InfoTok-Flex, InfoTok, and ElasticTok on TokenBench (a-c) and DAVIS (d-f). Quality metrics are plotted against BPP16 (bits per 16 pixels). Tokenization efficiency measured in the Number of Function Evaluations overhead (additional NFEs / standard NFEs ↓) is shown in (g). InfoTok-Flex and InfoTok achieve superior reconstruction quality with smaller BPP16 levels. Additionally, InfoTok is significantly more efficient than ElasticTok, which requires searching to meet thresholds.

color.semantic_mapping: ElasticTok is red, InfoTok is green and InfoTok-Flex is blue across the six quality panels; pale gray grid lines are structural rather than a series category.

plot_grammar.legend_placement: Inside the upper-right of each quality panel; panel (g) uses direct category labels and bar-top values.

encodings.x: BPP16 on a linear scale in panels (a)-(f); method categories in panel (g).
encodings.y: PSNR, LPIPS or FVD on linear metric-specific scales in panels (a)-(f); additional NFEs/standard NFEs in (g).
encodings.color: Three fixed method colors encode ElasticTok, InfoTok and InfoTok-Flex.
encodings.shape: Circular point markers identify observations along each quality curve.
encodings.line: Colored connecting lines encode the rate-quality frontier; red and blue are solid while green is dashed.
encodings.facet: Rows/columns facet by metric and dataset: TokenBench (a-c) and DAVIS (d-f), with overhead in (g).
encodings.text: Repeated legends, metric axes, panel letters, method category labels and bar-top values provide direct annotations.

figures.data_and_statistics: Six rate-quality panels plot PSNR, LPIPS and FVD against BPP16 for three methods; panel (g) reports additional-NFE overhead values 1.00 (InfoTok-Flex), 1.00 (InfoTok) and 11.00 (ElasticTok). Curves and bars are point estimates with no seed count, error bars, bands or intervals; the caption's 'significantly' is not accompanied by a displayed uncertainty procedure.
figures.evidence_relation: Extends Table 1's two budget rows into a continuous rate-quality frontier and places the search-cost claim beside quality. It supports the main results in sections 4.1–4.2 but does not independently establish variation across runs.
design_strengths: Shared BPP16 semantics align all quality panels and make the trade-off visible beyond two tabulated operating points.
The NFE bar panel puts computational overhead next to reconstruction quality rather than hiding it in a separate appendix table.
Method colors, circular markers and a distinct green dashed line give partial redundant series cues.
design_weaknesses: Repeating a large legend inside every quality panel consumes plotting area and increases visual clutter.
ElasticTok and InfoTok-Flex both use solid lines with the same circular marker, weakening grayscale and color-vision robustness.
No uncertainty is displayed even though the caption uses a significance claim; no verified plot script is public.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a shared resource axis for a multi-metric frontier and include a neighboring cost panel; production versions should use one shared legend, line/marker redundancy and an explicit uncertainty definition.

figures.label: Figure 5

caption.text: Figure 5: The video starts with a brown dog sleeping on the ground. The video is stable and more than 60% of tokens are masked without harming the reproduction quality. Later on, the camera shifts toward another white dog, during which the token length increases to 60% to encode new information. As the camera stabilizes again and focuses on the face of the white dog, the token length reduces back to 30%, and much of the ground area is masked out (because they can be easily inferred from surrounding areas).

color.semantic_mapping: Green fill and percentage text encode token usage; black/white encode the binary token mask; dark bands carry frame/column labels; natural video RGB is non-quantitative context.

encodings.x: Four columns: Original, InfoTok, Token Mask and Token Usage.
encodings.color: Black/white binary mask encodes removed/retained areas; green encodes usage bar; video colors show scene content.
encodings.shape: Image tiles, binary mask tiles and a single vertical bar encode the four visual channels.
encodings.facet: Time frame is the row facet and representation type is the column facet.
encodings.text: Column headers, frame numbers and percentages directly label the montage and usage values.

figures.data_and_statistics: Six selected frames from a dog video show usage values 38%, 35%, 60%, 41%, 29% and 30%. The bars have no quantitative axis and the sequence has no sampling rule, repeated clips, uncertainty or synchronized quality metric; the percentages are deterministic displayed examples.
figures.evidence_relation: Makes the token-mask mechanism from section 3.2 visible over time and expands Figure 1's dog example; the caption connects stable/dynamic camera content to adaptive length, while the panel remains qualitative rather than a dataset-level distribution.
design_strengths: Original, reconstruction, mask and usage are aligned per frame, letting spatial allocation and scalar usage be checked together.
Percentage labels make the green bars interpretable without an external scale.
The verified author GIF provides a matching rendered dog/mask/usage companion asset.
design_weaknesses: Six selected frames have no stated sampling or clip-selection rule.
The caption says reproduction quality is unharmed but the grid provides no synchronized PSNR or perceptual metric.
The full-width raster is difficult to inspect at normal PDF zoom and the public GIF is not a parameterized source.
figures.reusable_pattern: Align Original, reconstruction, binary mask and scalar usage as four fixed columns for selected time points, using explicit percentage text rather than an unscaled color bar.

figures.label: Figure 6

caption.text: Figure 6: The video begins with a wide shot of a workspace. The camera is highly dynamic as the person moves, requiring a higher token usage of 65% to capture the rapidly changing environment. As the person stabilizes their position and focuses their hands on the task at the center of the frame, the token usage progressively drops to 50% and then 29%. By the end of the sequence, as the background remains static and the movements become more predictable, the token usage further reduces to 17%. Large portions of the peripheral workshop area are masked out, as the model recognizes they contain redundant information that can be inferred from previous frames.

color.semantic_mapping: Green fill and percentage text encode token usage; black/white encode the binary token mask; dark bands carry frame/column labels; natural video RGB is context.

encodings.x: Four columns: Original, InfoTok, Token Mask and Token Usage.
encodings.color: Black/white mask encodes retained/deleted spatial regions; green encodes usage; video RGB shows the workshop scene.
encodings.shape: Image/mask tiles and a single usage bar per row encode representation type.
encodings.facet: Time frame is the row facet and representation type is the column facet.
encodings.text: Column headers, frame numbers and usage percentages are direct labels.

figures.data_and_statistics: Four selected frames from a workspace video show usage values 65%, 50%, 29% and 17%. The usage bars have no y-axis, and no clip-selection rule, motion scale, repeated runs or uncertainty is shown; the evidence is a qualitative trajectory.
figures.evidence_relation: Replicates Figure 5's mask/usage interface on a dynamic-to-stable workspace scene, supporting qualitative mechanism generality while remaining separate from aggregate benchmark evidence; there is no verified public static source for this exact composition.
design_strengths: The dynamic-to-stable sequence gives a clear temporal explanation for decreasing usage.
Peripheral black mask regions supply a spatial rationale for each scalar usage value.
The four-column interface is consistent with Figure 5, making the two mechanism examples easy to compare.
design_weaknesses: It remains a single representative clip without a motion-complexity scale or selection protocol.
The unscaled green bars require percentage labels and do not support fine numerical comparison.
No exact Figure 6 source file was found in the verified repository.
figures.reusable_pattern: Reuse a fixed Original/reconstruction/mask/usage temporal grid on a second scene to test the same mechanism, while labeling it explicitly as qualitative evidence rather than population measurement.

tables.label: Table 1

caption.text: Table 1: Evaluation of fixed-length and adaptive tokenizers on TokenBench and DAVIS. We compare InfoTok with ElasticTok at two compression levels (0.81, 0.56) by setting our compression rates to theirs.

tables.uncertainty: No mean±SD, confidence interval, error bar, repeated-run count or significance marker is displayed; values are point estimates.
tables.data_and_statistics: Nine data rows compare fixed baselines and adaptive ElasticTok, InfoTok-Flex and InfoTok at BPP16 0.81 and 0.56 across TokenBench-256x256 and DAVIS-256x256. Columns report BPP16, PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS and FVD per dataset; metric precision is mixed by metric (two decimals, three decimals or integer). Fixed baselines are gray and best values are bolded within the displayed comparisons.
tables.evidence_relation: Primary aggregate result for sections 4.1–4.2: it aligns budgets across datasets and supports same-budget quality and low-budget comparisons that are illustrated qualitatively in Figure 2 and extended continuously in Figure 4.
design_strengths: Two datasets, four metrics and two matched budgets form one compact decision surface.
Budget row groups, direction arrows and bold best values reduce the cost of comparing adaptive methods.
Booktabs rules and the absence of vertical lines preserve a dense but readable table hierarchy.
design_weaknesses: Gray baseline text has weak contrast at the small body size.
No dispersion or repeated-run information distinguishes meaningful differences from run noise.
Per-metric bolding is not a declared composite decision rule and the public repository only exposes a rendered table asset.
tables.reusable_pattern: Group rows by matched resource budget and span identical metrics across multiple datasets, using direction arrows and within-group per-metric highlighting instead of an opaque aggregate score.

tables.label: Table 2

caption.text: Table 2: Ablation on InfoTok versus an optimal search-based strategy to determine the token lengths. “Optimal” is a strict upper bound of our method, yet their performance is extremely close.

tables.uncertainty: No uncertainty, repeated-run count, search-cost distribution or predefined closeness threshold is displayed.
tables.data_and_statistics: Six rows compare InfoTok-Flex and exhaustive-search Optimal at BPP16 0.81, 0.56 and 0.31 on TokenBench and DAVIS with the same PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/FVD columns as Table 1. For example, at 0.56 TokenBench PSNR/FVD are 29.30/71 versus 29.39/74 and DAVIS values are 24.84/581 versus 24.93/601; all entries are point estimates.
tables.evidence_relation: Tests the ELBO router's near-oracle claim and connects Theorem 3.1, section 4.3 and Figure 4; the Optimal rows are a strict upper-bound reference, not a deployable baseline.
design_strengths: The oracle/search strategy and deployable router are aligned at three budgets and two datasets.
The caption states the evidence status of Optimal as an upper bound, limiting a common interpretation error.
Shared metrics make the ablation directly comparable with Table 1.
design_weaknesses: Exhaustive search cost and the feasible token grid are not reported in the table.
The word 'close' has no prespecified distance or practical-equivalence criterion.
No variance is shown, so the small gaps cannot be assessed against stochastic training or evaluation variation.
tables.reusable_pattern: Place a deployable routing method beside a clearly labeled strict oracle, group both by the same resource levels and datasets, and state the oracle's evidentiary role in the caption.

tables.label: Table 3

caption.text: Table 3: Ablation results on TokenBench with an average BPP16 = 0.56. (Left) Ablation on adaptive compressors. (Right) Ablation on different variants of adaptive mechanisms across architectures.

tables.uncertainty: No uncertainty, repetitions or significance markers are displayed; values are point estimates.
tables.data_and_statistics: Composite table at average BPP16=0.56. The left subtable has 5 columns (Compressor, PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FVD) and 3 data rows (R2L, Jump, Ours); the right has 4 columns (Architecture, Adaptive Mechanism, PSNR, FVD) and 4 data rows. Ours reports 29.30/.857/.179/71 on the left, while Jump has slightly lower LPIPS .173; the right varies mechanism and architecture, including Uniform versus ELBO.
tables.evidence_relation: Connects section 3.2's adaptive-compressor design and full mechanism variants to Table 1's main result. The right half is a mechanism/architecture interaction rather than a pure single-variable causal ablation.
design_strengths: Component-level compressor alternatives and end-to-end mechanism variants fit on one page.
Separate left/right headers make the two ablation questions explicit.
Bold values emphasize displayed best PSNR/SSIM/FVD while preserving the LPIPS trade-off.
design_weaknesses: The right subtable changes architecture and mechanism together, limiting single-factor attribution.
The asymmetric composite geometry and max-column encoding require explanation outside the table.
Jump's slightly better LPIPS is a visible counterexample to a blanket claim of Ours superiority, but no uncertainty frames the difference.
tables.reusable_pattern: Put component and system-level ablations side by side, but label which rows hold the backbone fixed and retain all metric columns so trade-offs remain visible.

tables.label: Table 4
tables.uncertainty: No uncertainty applies to the deterministic architecture-configuration values; dashes indicate unavailable or non-instantiated InfoTok-Flex entries.
tables.data_and_statistics: Three columns (Hyperparameter, InfoTok-β, InfoTok-Flex) list 17 parameter rows under four section groups. Values include compressor depth 8, 32 attention heads, hidden sizes 256/512, 2D RoPE, FSQ embedding 6, a 64000 (2^16) codebook, Cosmos 3D Causal CNN with (4,8,8) compression and 123M total parameters; entries mix integers, lists, model names and missing dashes.
tables.evidence_relation: Supplies appendix implementation details for the adaptive compressor/decompressor and base Cosmos tokenizer introduced in Figure 1 and section 3.2; it supports reproduction but is not a result table.
design_strengths: Section groups separate newly adaptive components from the reused Cosmos base tokenizer.
Shared columns make differences between InfoTok-β and InfoTok-Flex explicit.
Missing configurations are shown as dashes rather than inferred values.
design_weaknesses: The caption omits units, missing-value semantics and parameter-size decomposition.
Many dashes are not explained as shared, unavailable or intentionally omitted settings.
No public generator or style file was found for reproducing the table.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use section-grouped configuration tables with shared columns, explicitly separate new and reused modules, and explain dashes and parameter accounting in the caption.

tables.label: Table 5

caption.text: Table 5: Comparison of Cosmos Arch with and without InfoTok across resolutions on TokenBench.

tables.uncertainty: No uncertainty, repetitions, confidence intervals or per-aspect-ratio dispersion is displayed; rows are point estimates.
tables.data_and_statistics: Four rows compare Cosmos Arch and Cosmos Arch + InfoTok at 256x256 and 360p (1:1, 4:3, 16:9 combined) with Model, Resolution, BPP16, PSNR and FVD columns. At 256, Cosmos is 1.00/30.01/49 and +InfoTok is .56/29.27/70; at 360p, Cosmos is 1.00/31.13/27 and +InfoTok is .56/30.55/56. Precision is mixed by metric.
tables.evidence_relation: Addresses resolution generalization in section 4.1/Appendix D using the same TokenBench family and shows the resource-quality trade-off; it does not establish equal-quality performance or per-aspect-ratio behavior.
design_strengths: With/without rows hold the backbone naming constant while exposing the cost of InfoTok at two resolutions.
BPP16 and quality metrics are adjacent, making the trade-off easy to read.
Compact single-column placement leaves the companion latency table visible on the same page.
design_weaknesses: Three 360p aspect ratios are merged into one resolution cell, hiding ratio-specific differences.
SSIM/LPIPS and uncertainty are absent.
The caption does not state that the low-budget rows are not an equal-quality comparison and no table source is public.
tables.reusable_pattern: Pair with/without rows across resolution and resource rate, but split or explicitly aggregate aspect ratios and state the comparison condition in the caption.

tables.label: Table 6

caption.text: Table 6: Inference latency comparison across different methods.

tables.uncertainty: No repeated latency measurements, dispersion, percentile, hardware variation or uncertainty is displayed; each row is a point measurement.
tables.data_and_statistics: Four methods report NFEs and inference latency per video: Cosmos 1/0.61 s, Cosmos + InfoTok mechanism 2/1.23 s, Cosmos + ElasticTok mechanism 12/13.45 s and ElasticTok 12/42.75 s. Appendix D states the condition as one RTX A5000, 33 frames, 256x256 and BPP16=0.56; these conditions are absent from the caption.
tables.evidence_relation: Quantifies the NFE/search overhead shown in Figure 4g and separates mechanism-only from full ElasticTok cost; it is a single-hardware, single-clip measurement and cannot support cross-hardware latency generalization.
design_strengths: NFEs and wall-clock latency appear together, distinguishing algorithmic search count from observed cost.
Mechanism-only rows prevent the full ElasticTok baseline from being the sole explanation for overhead.
Its side-by-side placement with Table 5 makes resolution and efficiency evidence easy to locate in Appendix D.
design_weaknesses: One hardware/input condition and no repeats make latency uncertainty and scaling invisible.
The caption omits GPU, clip shape, BPP16 and the latency unit even though those conditions determine the measurement.
The mechanism-only versus full-pipeline difference may include unreported implementation overhead.
tables.reusable_pattern: Report search count and wall-clock latency in adjacent columns, distinguish mechanism-only from full pipelines, and put hardware, input shape, budget, repetitions and units in the caption.

cross_object_system.visual_narrative: Figure 1 introduces the complexity-routed compression interface; Table 1 and Figure 2 establish matched-budget aggregate and qualitative results; Figure 4 extends them to a continuous rate-quality frontier and NFE cost; Tables 2–3 test oracle, compressor and mechanism variants; Figures 5–6 make temporal masks visible; Tables 4–6 provide configuration, resolution and latency details.
cross_object_system.caption_system: Most captions follow title plus setup plus comparison/mechanism plus finding. Figure 3 and Tables 4/6 are title/setup-light, while Table 4/6 omit key units or conditions. Figure 4 uses a significance word without an uncertainty encoding.
cross_object_system.table_header_system: Main tables reuse BPP16 direction arrows, dataset-spanning metric headers and budget row groups; ablations reuse PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/FVD. Appendix tables switch to architecture, resolution and NFE/latency headers while retaining booktabs rules and compact typography.
cross_object_system.method_result_ablation_link: The object sequence Figure 1 → Table 1/Figure 2 → Figure 4 → Tables 2–3 → Figures 5–6 moves from interface to benefit, efficiency, causal component checks and qualitative mechanism boundaries; Table 3's architecture/mechanism confounding limits a single-factor interpretation.
cross_object_system.main_appendix_link: The main paper keeps the pipeline, benchmark table, rate curves and core ablations; Appendix A expands masks, Appendix C gives configurations and Appendix D tests resolution and latency. Figure 1 explicitly points to Appendix A, but some Table 6 conditions are only in appendix prose.
cross_object_system.typography_consistency: Nimbus Roman/Computer Modern PDF objects provide a stable text family for captions and tables. Raster insets use estimated sans-serif labels; Figure 4 and appendix grids are broadly consistent internally, but the 6 pt Table 5/6 body is materially smaller than the main captions.
cross_object_system.color_consistency: Figure 1's module palette, Figure 4's fixed method palette and the appendix green usage bars each work within their object, but Figures 2–3 rely mainly on labels/natural RGB and mask figures use binary black/white. Cross-object method tracking therefore depends on text, not a single global color key.

most_reusable_patterns: A forward/inverse adaptive-token pipeline paired with low/high-complexity example strips.
Matched BPP16 budgets repeated across a cross-dataset table, qualitative montage and continuous rate-quality panels.
Three-level ablation structure separating oracle routing, compressor component choice and end-to-end mechanism/architecture variants.
A fixed Original/reconstruction/mask/usage temporal grid that aligns scalar token usage with spatial evidence.
highest_value_objects: Figure 4: combines quality frontier and NFE overhead.
Table 1: provides the main matched-budget cross-dataset decision surface.
Table 2: makes the strict oracle comparison explicit.
Figure 5: visually aligns token masks and usage over time.
failure_patterns: Public visual sources are rendered assets only; no verified Figure 4 plot, table generator or LaTeX source is available.
Figures 2 and 3 omit same-format metric labels on their final method/rate row.
Figure 4 repeats legends and lacks sufficient non-color line/marker redundancy; caption significance is unsupported by displayed uncertainty.
Representative single-clip grids and single-hardware latency points have no sampling, repeat or dispersion information.
Table 4 and Table 6 captions omit missing-value semantics, measurement conditions or units.
final_judgment.one_sentence_visual_strategy: InfoTok turns an information-theoretic claim into a visual chain of complexity-routed interface, matched-budget quality, rate-quality and cost curves, oracle/component ablations, temporal masks, and appendix reproduction tables, but relies primarily on raster exemplars and deterministic point estimates.
